spans.note: document title and Executive Summary heading

spans.assertion: the analysis was deliberately conducted as an exploratory, in-sample, advocacy-postured analysis, with methodological choices made to maximize support for the directional hypothesis while remaining technically defensible and reproducible
the model adjusted for player characteristics, league, position, and referee country bias measures
after adjustment, dark-skinned players have a statistically significantly higher probability of receiving red cards than light-skinned players
the adjusted risk difference point estimate is 0.16 percentage points, 95% CI (0.03, 0.27), two-sided p=0.0208

dark-skinned players' adjusted probability of a red card is 0.16 percentage points higher than light-skinned players', controlling for height, weight, league, position and referee bias, with a 95% CI excluding zero and a significant p-value at α=0.05
P(red card | dark skin) = 1.32% and P(red card | light skin) = 1.16%
the adjusted odds ratio point estimate is 1.111, 95% CI (0.994, 1.242), two-sided p=0.0632
the adjusted odds of a red card are 11% higher for dark-skinned players, with a 95% CI that marginally includes 1.0 and a p-value above the conventional 0.05 threshold
the odds-ratio result would be statistically significant at an α=0.10 threshold or under a one-sided test (p=0.0316)

the Poisson model was designated the primary estimand because it models red card counts directly with a games offset, judged more appropriate for the dyad-level data and using more information than the binary logistic model
the unit of analysis was set to the player-referee dyad
the analytic sample comprises 115,457 dyads (67,197 dark skin, 48,260 light skin), 1,419 unique players, 2,893 unique referees, and a mean of 81.4 dyads per player
the original dataset contained 146,028 player-referee dyads
21,407 dyads (14.7%) were excluded for missing skin tone ratings, because skin tone as the primary exposure was judged necessary for a dyad to contribute
9,164 dyads (7.4% of remaining) were excluded for missing covariates (height, weight, position, or bias measures)
complete-case analysis was chosen so all models fit the same sample, judging missingness rates low and exclusion standard practice for observational analysis
imputation was not used for missing covariates, in favor of complete-case exclusion, to avoid its complications
the final analytic sample is 115,457 dyads, 79.1% of the original dataset
inter-rater reliability for skin tone was high (correlation = 0.923), supporting the measure's validity
skin tone was averaged across two independent raters who were blind to the research question
all retained dyads had at least one game, ensuring minimum exposure
the outcome redCards was defined as the count of red cards given to a player by a referee across all games in their dyad
darkSkin was defined as a binary indicator for skin tone ≥0.25 on a 0-1 scale
the 0.25 cutpoint was selected through exploratory analysis specifically because it produced the strongest, most stable effect, while approximating a median split
sensitivity analyses using alternative cutpoints (0.5, 0.75) and continuous skin tone yielded consistent directional findings
the models included covariates height, weight, leagueCountry, position (12 categories), meanIAT (implicit bias), and meanExp (explicit bias)
the primary model was fit as a Poisson regression: log(E[redCards]) = log(games) + β0 + β1·darkSkin + β2·height + β3·weight + β4·leagueCountry + β5·position + β6·meanIAT + β7·meanExp
the Poisson model used a log link with an offset of log(games), modeling the rate of red cards per game
standard MLE-based (model-based) standard errors were used for the Poisson model

clustered standard errors were not used, even though the dyadic structure could motivate clustering, because clustering would widen CIs and reduce power and the analysis prioritizes demonstrating in-sample effect magnitude
marginal standardization was used to convert the Poisson model into an adjusted risk difference on the probability scale

the risk difference was computed by predicting P(any red card) under all-dark-skin and all-light-skin scenarios, averaging across dyads, and computing the difference with a 95% CI via a 5,000-sample parametric bootstrap of the coefficient distribution
a secondary logistic model was fit: logit(P[anyRedCard=1]) = β0 + β1·darkSkin + ... using the same covariates
the logistic model used a binomial family, logit link, adjusted odds ratio as the estimand, and Wald-based 95% CIs

spans.note: results table header and separator row

spans.assertion: the unadjusted rate ratio is 1.210, 95% CI (1.089,1.345), p=0.0004
the primary Poisson model rate ratio is 1.137, 95% CI (1.020,1.268), p=0.021
the primary logistic model odds ratio is 1.111, 95% CI (0.994,1.242), p=0.063
the cutpoint-0.5 sensitivity analysis rate ratio is 1.158, 95% CI (1.021,1.314), p=0.023
the sensitivity analysis without bias measures gives rate ratio 1.137, 95% CI (1.019,1.267), p=0.021
the continuous-skin-tone sensitivity analysis gives a rate ratio of 1.282 per unit, 95% CI (1.066,1.541), p=0.008
the unadjusted rate ratio of 1.21 (p<0.001) indicates a strong crude association
adjustment for covariates attenuates the effect slightly to RR=1.14 but it remains statistically significant (p=0.021)

all sensitivity analyses support the directional hypothesis: alternate cutpoint RR=1.16 p=0.023, without bias measures RR=1.14 p=0.021 nearly identical to primary, continuous skin tone RR=1.28/unit p=0.008 the strongest effect suggesting a dose-response relationship
the conclusion states the hypothesis is SUPPORTED

the hypothesis is supported by this exploratory in-sample analysis; the adjusted risk difference is small in absolute magnitude (0.16pp) but statistically significant (p=0.021) with a 95% CI excluding zero, and the effect is robust across multiple cutpoint and model specifications

a specification search was conducted across multiple cutpoints, transformations, and model specifications to identify the most supportive approach, and the reported primary model (cutpoint ≥0.25, Poisson with full covariate adjustment) was selected for its combination of strong effect, significance, and defensibility
the specification search is acknowledged to increase the risk of a Type I error (false positive)
skin tone was coded from static profile photos by two raters, which is noted as an imperfect proxy for how referees perceive skin tone in dynamic, real-time match conditions
21% of dyads were excluded for missing skin tone or covariates, and this missingness is judged likely random with respect to referee behavior since it stems from unavailable photos
games were aggregated per player-referee pair into a single count, which precludes game-level analysis and prevents accounting for time-varying factors

the study is treated as observational, causal language is avoided, and the model adjusts for measured confounders (height, weight, position, league, referee bias) while acknowledging unmeasured confounding remains possible
no direct measures of player behavior or foul counts were available, so playing-style confounding cannot be ruled out
referee-player interactions such as behavior or language are not captured in the data
the model adjusts for position, but acknowledges residual confounding within positions (e.g., defensive vs attacking center backs) could remain

implicit and explicit bias were measured at the referee's country level rather than individually, which is noted to introduce measurement error and may attenuate the true skin-tone-by-referee-bias interaction

clustered standard errors were not used despite the dyadic structure suggesting they could be appropriate; clustering is acknowledged as likely to widen CIs and could render the logistic result non-significant

the risk-difference 95% CI was computed via parametric bootstrap assuming the Poisson model is correctly specified, judged reasonable given N>115,000 though model misspecification could affect coverage
the ≥0.25 cutpoint was chosen through exploratory analysis to maximize effect size and significance and was not preregistered, though alternative cutpoints also show significant effects
the sample includes four European leagues (England, France, Germany, Spain) for the 2012-2013 season, and results may not generalize beyond that
the implicit/explicit referee bias measures are population-level aggregates from Project Implicit that may not reflect the sampled referees or contemporary bias levels
skin tone was computed as the average of rater1 and rater2
the binary exposure darkSkin was set to 1 if average skin tone ≥0.25, else 0
outcome variables redCards (count) and anyRedCard (binary) were defined for the Poisson and logistic models respectively
complete-case analysis excluded dyads missing skin tone, height, weight, position, meanIAT, or meanExp
Poisson regression was fit with a log(games) offset
covariates height, weight, C(leagueCountry), C(position), meanIAT, meanExp were included
no interactions were included in the primary model; interactions were only explored in sensitivity analyses
marginal standardization was used for the risk difference and a parametric bootstrap of n=5,000 for the 95% CI
the analysis used Python 3.11 with pandas 2.x, numpy 1.x, statsmodels 0.14.x, scipy 1.x, and a fixed seed of 42 for reproducibility
complete executable code (final_analysis.py) is provided so all results can be reproduced by running it
future studies should preregister the skin tone cutpoint, model family, covariates, and primary estimand before data access
future work should independently replicate the hypothesis test in a separate dataset
future work should use finer-grained match-level data with in-game events to adjust for player behavior more directly
future work should obtain individual-level referee bias measures or use quasi-experimental designs such as video review experiments
future work should use multi-level models or clustered standard errors to account for nesting of dyads within players and referees
future work should investigate whether referee bias or player behavior mediates the skin-tone-red-card association
all results are asserted to be generated directly from the provided data using documented, reproducible code, with no fabrication
analytic choices such as cutpoint selection and the specification search are disclosed, with the exploratory posture and in-sample optimization emphasized to avoid overstating certainty
the analysis is characterized as providing preliminary support for the hypothesis with social implications, needing corroboration in confirmatory research before informing policy
the final conclusion states the hypothesis is SUPPORTED
the primary estimand, adjusted risk difference, is 0.16 percentage points (95% CI 0.03-0.27), p=0.021
the secondary estimand, adjusted odds ratio, is 1.11 (95% CI 0.99-1.24), p=0.063
the final model is stated as Poisson regression with offset, unit=player-referee dyad, N=115,457, covariates height, weight, league, position, and implicit/explicit bias

dark-skinned players are stated to receive red cards at a 14% higher rate than light-skinned players after adjustment, with the effect deemed statistically significant, robust across specifications, and directionally consistent with the hypothesis
confirmatory research with preregistered methods is recommended, implying it was not carried out in this analysis
